turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning, Mrs Hale. Coat on the chair if you like. I'll do your checks before Dr Adeyemi calls you in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, yes. Sorry, I'm a bit wound up. My daughter had to park miles off.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): That's alright. Blood pressure today is one oh nine over seventy-seven. Your last pressure was one-forty, so today's a bit softer.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Softer. Right. Is softer bad?
[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Not on its own. Pulse, uh, I nearly called it eighty-eight, sorry, it's seventy-six beats a minute. Temperature thirty-eight point three degrees.
[SEG0006] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Weight next. Err, fifty-four, no, the scales say fifty-two kilograms. Last time in March you were sixty-eight.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I've gone thin then. I haven't been eating proper since the op, not really.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello Mrs Hale, I'm Dr Adeyemi. I've got the figures from outside. What brings you in?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): The six week check, after my hip. The right one. I keep thinking something's not right.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Six weeks on from the right hip replacement. How has it actually been?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): The scar looks closed to me. But it aches, umm, especially in the evening, and I'm still on the stick the whole time.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): I saw you come along on the stick. Evening ache. Any swelling in the calf?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No swelling. I keep looking and the calf's not swollen.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or trouble getting your breath?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. Breathing's been fine.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): And your waterworks, any stinging or trouble passing urine?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's all normal, honestly.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you felt feverish at home?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, I don't think so. Well, actually, I felt a bit warm in the evenings, but I never took it, so I don't know.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): A bit warm in the evenings, and you're not sure it was a real fever. What are you taking?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Aspirin, a hundred and fifty milligrams, once a day, for the clots. And paracetemol, the five hundred milligram tablets, two of them four times a day, for the ache.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll say that back. Aspirin one hundred and fifty milligrams once a day for the clots, paracetamol one gram four times a day for the hip ache. Have you stopped anything?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): The codeine. Thirty milligrams at night. I stopped that about a week ago. It made me all fuzzy.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Codeine thirty milligrams at night, stopped a week ago. Any other tablets of your own?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No. My sister keeps on at me to take biotin, like she does for her nails, but I don't. And my husband was on metformin for his diabetes. That's his, not mine.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Biotin is your sister's, and the metformin is your husband's, for his diabetes. Neither goes on your list.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. Only, is the aspirin dangerous? How long do I stay on it? I was reading online and I got myself in a proper state.

[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): After a hip replacement we often use it for about six weeks, so you're nearly through. Finish the box you've got, then stop. Don't stop halfway through the strip if you've a few days left.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Finish the box, then stop. What if a clot happens after?

[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the calf swells, or you get a sudden pain in the chest, or you can't get your breath, don't sit on it. Get help the same day. The calf isn't swollen today, which is reassuring.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): And the temperature, thirty-eight point three, is the hip infected? Please tell me straight.

[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look at the wound. It's healed, it's dry, there's no redness and there's no ooze. I don't think this is a wound infection. The temperature is a bit up and I'm not sure of the reason. It may be nothing much.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Not the hip, then. Can I have a bath? And can I drive? My daughter's been ferrying me and I hate having to ask.

[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): A bath is alright if you get in and out without twisting. Driving, I nearly said not while you're on codeine, but you've come off it. Give it another week, off the stick indoors first, before you try an emergency stop.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Another week. If I bend for something, will the new hip pop out? I dropped a spoon and I just froze.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): It can come out of joint if you fold right over and twist, so no bending past a right angle for a few more weeks. Leave the spoon, or use a grabber.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): I've got one. The night ache, is that still normal, though?

[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): A bit of ache at six weeks is common, evenings especially. Take the paracetamol regularly rather than chasing it. If the pain suddenly gets much worse, or the wound opens, ring us.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Regular paracetemol. I live on my own, mind. My daughter only pops round. What if I can't reach the phone?

[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Useful to know you live alone. Keep the phone next to the chair. Let me pull it together. Six weeks after the right hip replacement, wound healed, walking with a stick, evening ache, no calf swelling, no cough, waterworks fine, warm in the evenings but no clear fever. Aspirin one fifty until the box is finished, paracetamol one gram four times a day, codeine stopped. Temperature today 38.3, blood pressure 109 over 77, weight 52 kilograms. Heavier back in March, and I'm not chasing the weight today.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): You won't do bloods? I thought with that temperature you might.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): No bloods today. I will get an x-ray of the right hip while you're here, to check the position of the joint. And I'll see you back in three months.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Three months. If I'm worried before then I can ring, can't I?
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): If it's not settling, or you're properly feverish, ring and we'll see you sooner. Otherwise the three month visit stands.
[SEG0045] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll book the x-ray now and the three month slot. They'll call you from room two, Mrs Hale.

spec.situation: Older patient six weeks after a hip replacement with a daughter; wound healed; walks with a stick; takes aspirin for clots and painkiller; swelling of the calf asked about and denied.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Husband's diabetes is not family history.
Stopped codeine 30 mg at night is supported; frequency 'at night' not explicit as regular dosing.
bad.text: codeine (dose=30 mg, frequency=at night, status=discontinued, reported_by=patient)

bad.reason: Uncertain fever is supported; transcript does not mention uncertainty about when it began.
bad.text: The patient felt warm in the evenings but could not say whether it was a fever or when it began. (type=date_uncertain, related_entities=symptoms[1], resolution_status=unresolved)

omissions.text: Stopped codeine about a week ago because it made her feel 'fuzzy'.
Doctor advised no bending past a right angle for a few more weeks because the hip can dislocate if she folds right over and twists; use a grabber/leave dropped items.
Doctor advised she can drive only after another week and once she is off the stick indoors first, before trying an emergency stop.
Doctor advised same-day help if she gets sudden chest pain, in addition to calf swelling or breathlessness.
Examination finding that the right hip wound was dry was stated explicitly.
Doctor stated no blood tests would be done today.
Recorded family history is wrong: diabetes was mentioned as her husband's condition/medication, not a family history for the patient.
